paraphrase: Yoga is samādhi, and samādhi is a property of the mind at all its levels. The levels of the mind are the scattered (kṣipta), the stupefied (mūḍha), the distracted (vikṣipta), the one-pointed (ekāgra) and the stilled (niruddha). Samādhi in a distracted mind, being subordinate to distraction, does not count as yoga. Samādhi in a one-pointed mind, which illumines a real object, weakens the afflictions, loosens the bonds of karma and turns toward stilling, is called samprajñāta yoga (with reasoning, reflection, bliss or I-am-ness); when all activities are stilled, it is asamprajñāta samādhi.

paraphrase: The mind, having the nature of illumination, activity and inertia, has three guṇas. Mixed with rajas and tamas it loves power and objects; pervaded by tamas it tends to demerit, ignorance, attachment and powerlessness; with the veil of delusion gone and touched by rajas it tends to merit, knowledge, dispassion and power; freed from the last stain of rajas and established in itself it is only the discernment of the difference between sattva and puruṣa and tends to the meditation called the cloud of dharma — which meditators call the highest reflection (prasaṃkhyāna). The power of consciousness is unchanging, does not pass over [into objects], has objects shown to it, and is pure and infinite; discriminative discernment, being of the nature of sattva, is its opposite. Detached even from that discernment, the mind restrains it too; only impressions then remain: this is seedless samādhi, called asamprajñāta because nothing is cognized in it.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: In emergence the puruṣa has activities no different from the mind's. The mind, like a magnet, serves the puruṣa, its owner, by mere proximity, by being seen; their beginningless relation is the cause of the puruṣa's awareness of the mind's activities.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Afflicted activities are caused by the afflictions and become the field in which karmic residue accumulates; unafflicted ones have discernment as their object and oppose the operation of the guṇas. Unafflicted activities occur even in a stream of afflicted ones, and afflicted ones in the gaps of unafflicted ones. Activities make impressions and impressions make activities: so the wheel of activity and impression turns ceaselessly, until the mind, its task complete, abides as the self does, or dissolves.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Perception is the mind's activity, coloured by an external thing through the channel of the senses, that chiefly ascertains the particular in an object having general and particular aspects; its result is the puruṣa's awareness of the mind's activity. Inference chiefly ascertains the general, by a relation present in like cases and absent in unlike ones (the moon and stars move, because they change place, like Caitra). Testimony is the activity arising in a hearer from the words of a reliable speaker who has seen or inferred the matter; if the original speaker had not seen or inferred it, the testimony wavers.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Error is not valid cognition because valid cognition sublates it, as seeing one moon sublates seeing two. This is five-jointed ignorance — ignorance, I-am-ness, attachment, aversion and clinging — which under their own names are darkness (tamas), delusion (moha), great delusion (mahāmoha), gloom (tāmisra) and blinding gloom (andhatāmisra).
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Sleep is a particular cognition, because on waking it is recollected: 'I slept happily; my mind is clear'; 'I slept badly; my mind is dull and wanders'; 'I slept heavily, stupefied; my limbs are heavy'. Without an experience of cognition there could be no such recollection. In samādhi sleep too must be stilled, like other cognitions.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: The river of the mind flows both ways: it flows toward good and flows toward evil. Borne toward kaivalya and sloping toward discrimination, it flows toward good; borne toward saṃsāra and sloping toward non-discrimination, toward evil. Dispassion dams the stream toward objects; practice in seeing discrimination opens the stream of discrimination. So stilling depends on both.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Practice cultivated for a long time, without interruption and with devotion — accomplished with austerity, celibacy, knowledge and faith — becomes firmly grounded and is not quickly overpowered by the impressions of emergence.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Lower dispassion is the consciousness of mastery — without engagement, with nothing to reject or take up — of a mind that, by the strength of reflection, sees the faults of objects, whether seen (women, food and drink, power) or heard of in scripture (heaven, the bodiless state, absorption in prakṛti), even when in contact with divine or earthly objects.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Higher dispassion belongs to one who, seeing the faults of seen and scriptural objects, and with understanding nourished by the practice of seeing the puruṣa, is detached from the guṇas themselves, manifest and unmanifest. It is only the clarity of knowledge; when it arises the yogin thinks: 'What was to be attained is attained; the afflictions to be destroyed are destroyed; the close-jointed chain of becoming — by whose continuance one is born and dies, dies and is born — is cut.' Dispassion is the utmost limit of knowledge, and kaivalya is inseparable from it.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Reasoning (vitarka) is the mind's gross engagement with its support; reflection (vicāra) the subtle; bliss (ānanda) is joy; I-am-ness (asmitā) is awareness of a single self. The first samādhi, with reasoning, is accompanied by all four; the second, lacking reasoning, is with reflection; the third, lacking reflection, is with bliss; the fourth, lacking that, is I-am-ness alone. All these samādhis have a support.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: When all activities have set, the stilling of the mind with only impressions remaining is asamprajñāta samādhi; its means is higher dispassion. Practice with a support cannot achieve it, so the cognition of cessation, which has no object, is made the support; preceded by its practice the mind becomes without support, as if non-existent: this is seedless samādhi.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: The bodiless, who are gods, experience as it were the state of kaivalya with a mind that uses only its own impressions, and pass through the ripening of those impressions; likewise those merged in prakṛti, while the mind still has a task and is dissolved in prakṛti, experience as it were the state of kaivalya, until the mind returns by force of its unfinished task.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: For yogins [samādhi] comes from means. Faith is the serenity of the mind; like a kind mother it protects the yogin. In one who has faith and seeks discrimination, energy arises; in one with energy, mindfulness is present; with mindfulness present the mind, undisturbed, becomes concentrated; to the concentrated mind comes discerning insight, by which one knows things as they are. From practising that, and from dispassion toward its objects, asamprajñāta samādhi arises. These yogins are of nine kinds: mild, middling or intense in means, each with mild, middling or intense ardor.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked). The phrase 'smṛtyupasthāne' ('when mindfulness is present') is noted by scholars as Buddhist-sounding vocabulary (see brw:buddhism-yoga-five-faculties).

paraphrase: Won over by devotion (praṇidhāna), a special form of bhakti, Īśvara favours the yogin by his mere intention; from that intention alone the attainment of samādhi and its fruit is nearest for the yogin.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Afflictions, good and bad actions, their fruit and the residues exist in the mind but are ascribed to the puruṣa, as victory or defeat of soldiers is ascribed to their lord. Īśvara is the special puruṣa untouched by such experience. He is not like the liberated, who had an earlier state of bondage, nor like those merged in prakṛti, who may be bound later: he is always free and always the Lord. His eternal pre-eminence rests on his taking up of excellent sattva; scripture is its evidence, and scripture rests on that sattva, a beginningless relation. His lordship has no equal and no superior: two equal lords wishing opposite things at once could not both succeed; so he in whom lordship reaches its limit is Īśvara.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: The seed of omniscience — the supersensible grasp, lesser or greater, of past, future and present, singly or together — grows; where it is unsurpassed is the omniscient one, for what admits of degrees has a limit, like magnitude. Inference establishes only the general; his name and particulars must be sought from scripture. Though he has no purpose of his own, his purpose is compassion for beings: 'At the dissolutions I will lift up transmigrating beings by teaching knowledge and dharma.' So it is said: 'The first knower, the blessed supreme sage, out of compassion assumed a created mind and taught the doctrine to Āsuri, who wished to know.'
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked). The quoted sentence is attributed to Pañcaśikha by the commentators; the 'first knower' is taken to be Kapila.

paraphrase: Former teachers are limited by time; he, to whom time does not apply as a limit, is the teacher even of the ancients. As he is established in pre-eminence at the beginning of this creation, so he is to be understood at the beginning of past creations.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Īśvara is what the praṇava designates. The relation of designator and designated is not made by convention but stands fixed, like that of a lamp and its light; convention only shows the relation as it stands, as the relation of father and son is shown by 'this is his father, this his son'. In other creations too the convention is made in dependence on the same capacity; the upholders of scripture hold that the relation of word and meaning is eternal because usage is eternal.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: [Its repetition means] the repetition of the praṇava and the contemplation of Īśvara whom it designates; for the yogin who repeats the praṇava and contemplates its meaning the mind becomes one-pointed. So it is said: 'From self-study one should take to yoga, from yoga turn to self-study; through the perfection of self-study and yoga the supreme self shines forth.'
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Through devotion to Īśvara the obstacles such as illness do not arise, and one sees one's own nature: as Īśvara is a puruṣa pure, clear, alone and untroubled, so one comes to know the puruṣa who is witness to one's own buddhi.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: The nine obstacles are distractions of the mind that occur together with its activities. Illness is imbalance of the bodily elements, fluids and organs; dullness, the mind's unfitness for work; doubt, a cognition touching both alternatives; carelessness, failure to cultivate the means of samādhi; laziness, inactivity from heaviness of body and mind; non-abstention, the mind's greed for contact with objects; erroneous vision, false knowledge; failure to gain a stage, not reaching a level of samādhi; instability, the mind's not being established in a level gained. They are called the impurities of yoga, the adversaries of yoga, the obstacles to yoga.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Suffering is threefold — from oneself, from other beings and from the gods — that which beings, struck by it, strive to remove. Dejection is agitation of mind from thwarted desire; trembling is what shakes the limbs; inhalation is the breath drawing in outer air, exhalation the expelling of inner air. These occur in a distracted mind, not in a concentrated one.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: To counter distraction the mind should practise resting on a single principle. If the mind were only momentary cognitions each fixed to one object, every mind would be one-pointed and none distracted; and a stream of momentary cognitions has no single mind to which one-pointedness could belong. Hence the mind is one, has many objects, and endures. Otherwise, how could one cognition remember what another saw, or experience karma stored by another? And the self-experienced cognition 'I who saw now touch' requires one cognizer, and perception is not overruled by other means of knowledge.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: One should cultivate friendliness toward all beings who are happy, compassion toward the suffering, gladness toward the virtuous and equanimity toward the non-virtuous. By such cultivation white dharma arises; then the mind becomes clear, and the clear mind, one-pointed, attains steadiness.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Concentrating on the tip of the nose one becomes aware of divine smell; at the tip of the tongue, of taste; at the palate, of form; at the middle of the tongue, of touch; at the root of the tongue, of sound. These activities bind the mind to steadiness, dispel doubt and become a door to the insight of samādhi. Although what is learned from scripture, inference and a teacher's instruction is true, as long as not even a part of it is known by one's own faculties it does not produce firm conviction about subtle matters such as liberation; therefore some particular object must be made directly perceived, and then everything up to liberation is believed.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Concentrating on the lotus of the heart there arises awareness of the buddhi; the buddhi-sattva is luminous, like space, and through skill in steadiness the activity takes forms like the light of the sun, moon, planets and gems. Likewise the mind absorbed in I-am-ness becomes like a waveless ocean, calm, endless, I-am-ness alone. As it is said: 'having found that self, atomic in size, one knows only this: I am.' This twofold activity — with an object, and I-am-ness alone — is called sorrowless and luminous.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: As a flawless crystal takes on the colour of what it rests on, the mind coloured by a support and absorbed in it appears in the form of that support — gross elements, subtle elements, the variegated world; likewise the grasping senses, the grasping puruṣa, and even the liberated puruṣa. This taking on of the form of what it rests on is called coalescence (samāpatti).
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Word, object and cognition ('cow' as sound, as thing, as knowledge) are ordinarily grasped undivided though they are distinct. When the object that arises in the yogin's samādhi-insight is permeated by the constructions of word, object and cognition, that mixed coalescence is 'with reasoning'. When, memory of verbal convention being purified, the object stands in samādhi-insight in its own form alone, free of the constructions of testimony and inference, it is 'beyond reasoning': that is the highest perception, the seed of testimony and inference.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: The object of coalescence beyond reasoning is the whole (avayavin) — one, large or small, tangible, active and impermanent — through which ordinary dealings take place. For one who holds that the aggregate is unreal and the subtle cause imperceptible, there would be no whole, all cognition would be false, and then what would right knowledge be? Therefore the whole exists.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: The subtle object of an atom of earth is the smell-tanmātra (and so for water, fire, air and space); of these, I-am-ness; of this, the mere mark; of that, the unmarked; there is nothing subtler than the unmarked. The puruṣa is subtle too, but not so: it is not the material cause of the mark, only a [final] cause.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: When lucidity arises — a clear, steady flow of the luminous buddhi-sattva freed of the impurity of covering and not overpowered by rajas and tamas — the yogin has inner clarity, a clear light of insight that has real things as its object and does not follow sequence. As it is said: 'Having climbed the clarity of insight, the wise one, himself beyond sorrow, looks upon all sorrowing people as one standing on a mountain looks upon those on the ground.'
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked). The quoted verse parallels Dhammapada 28 (see brw:buddhism-yoga-shared-verses).

paraphrase: The insight born in that concentrated mind is called truth-bearing, aptly: it bears only truth, without a trace of error. As it is said: 'Refining insight in three ways — by scripture, by inference and by delight in the practice of meditation — one attains the highest yoga.'
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: The impression born of samādhi-insight obstructs the store of impressions of emergence; then cognitions from those do not arise, samādhi is present, and from it new insight and new impressions. These insight-made impressions do not give the mind a further task: since they cause the destruction of afflictions they bring it to rest, for the mind's activity ends in discernment.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: The impression born of stilling obstructs even the samādhi-born impressions; its existence is inferred from the experience of the duration of stilling. With the impressions of emergence, of stilling and of samādhi, which conduce to kaivalya, the mind dissolves into its own prakṛti; when the mind, its task ended, ceases, the puruṣa is established in its own form alone and is therefore called pure, alone and liberated.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: [Pāda 1 taught yoga for the concentrated mind; now how one with an emergent, unconcentrated mind may also be yoked to yoga.] Yoga does not succeed for one without austerity: impurity, variegated by beginningless karma, afflictions and latent tendencies and presenting a net of objects, is not broken up without it. Austerity is to be practised so as not to disturb the clarity of the mind. Self-study is the repetition of purifying [formulas] such as the praṇava, or the study of scriptures on liberation. Devotion to Īśvara is offering all actions to the supreme teacher, or renouncing their fruit.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Practised, kriyā-yoga cultivates samādhi and thins the afflictions; the thinned afflictions, burnt by the fire of reflection (prasaṃkhyāna) like seeds, become unable to sprout; then subtle insight — only the discernment of the difference between sattva and puruṣa, untouched by afflictions, its task complete — becomes fit for dissolution.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: The afflictions are the five errors; when active they strengthen the dominion of the guṇas, establish transformation, raise the stream of cause and effect and, supporting one another, bring about the fruition of karma.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Ignorance is the breeding-ground of the other four, which may be dormant, thinned, interrupted or active. Dormancy is existence in the mind as mere potency, as seeds; awakening is their facing an object. In one who possesses reflection, whose affliction-seeds are burnt, they do not arise again even when the object is present — how could a burnt seed sprout? Hence one whose afflictions are exhausted is called 'skilled' (kuśala) and 'in his last body'; in him alone is this fifth, burnt-seed state of the afflictions. Thinned: weakened by cultivating the opposite. Interrupted: arising again and again in alternation, as anger is not active while attachment is. Active: operating on an object. All the afflictions are forms of ignorance, cling to what ignorance has shaped, and dwindle as it dwindles.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Taking effects that are impermanent as permanent ('the earth is fixed, the sky with moon and stars is fixed, the gods are immortal'); taking the utterly foul body as pure — 'because of its place, its seed, its support, its discharges, its end, and its need of cleansing, the wise know the body as impure' — as when a girl is seen as made of honey and nectar; taking the painful as pleasant; taking the non-self — outer things, the body, the mind — as the self: 'whoever takes sattva, manifest or unmanifest, as the self, rejoicing in its prosperity and grieving at its misfortune as his own, is unawakened.' Ignorance thus has four feet and is the root of the stream of afflictions and of karmic residue with its fruition. Like 'non-friend' (amitra), it is not the absence of knowledge nor mere knowledge, but another cognition contrary to knowledge.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: The puruṣa is the power of seeing, the buddhi the power of sight; their appearing as one nature is the affliction I-am-ness. Experience happens when enjoyer and enjoyable, utterly distinct and unmixed, seem undivided; when their own forms are discerned there is kaivalya — how then experience? As it is said: 'Not seeing the puruṣa beyond the buddhi, distinct in form, character and knowledge, one takes the buddhi for the self through delusion.'
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Every living being always has this wish for itself: 'May I not cease to be; may I be.' It cannot belong to one who has never experienced death, so it shows the experience of a former birth. This affliction, clinging, flowing by its own momentum, a fear of death of the nature of the view of annihilation, not produced by perception, inference or testimony, is found even in a worm just born; and it is established in the wise, who know the before and after, as much as in the most deluded.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: The gross activities of the afflictions, thinned by kriyā-yoga, are to be abandoned by reflection, by meditation, until they are made subtle, like burnt seeds. As the gross dirt of cloth is shaken off first and the fine dirt removed afterwards with effort and means, so the gross activities have small antidotes, the subtle ones great antidotes.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: The store of meritorious and demeritorious karma arises from desire, greed, delusion and anger, and ripens in this birth or another. Merit accomplished with intense ardor through mantra, austerity and samādhi, or by worship of Īśvara, gods, great sages and great beings, ripens at once; so does demerit from repeated harm to the frightened, the sick and the wretched, to those who trusted, or to great beings and ascetics — as the boy Nandīśvara was transformed from a man into a god, and Nahuṣa, king of the gods, into an animal. Hell-beings have no karmic residue to be experienced in the present birth; those whose afflictions are exhausted have none to be experienced in a future birth.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: While afflictions exist the karmic residue begins to ripen; once their root is cut it does not — as rice in its husk, its seed-state unburnt, can sprout, but husked or burnt rice cannot. The fruition is threefold: birth, life-span and experience. One deed is not the cause of one birth, nor one deed of many births, nor many deeds of many births; rather the varied mass of merit and demerit accumulated between birth and death, manifested at death, brings about a single birth, with its life-span and experience: this residue is said to be 'of one life' (ekabhavika).

paraphrase: Every pleasure is pervaded by attachment and dependent on means, so there is karmic residue from attachment, and likewise from aversion and delusion; and 'enjoyment is impossible without harming beings'. Dispassion cannot be made by indulgence, for attachments and the senses' skill grow with it — like one afraid of a scorpion's sting who is bitten by a snake. So there are the sufferings of change, of anguish and of impressions, a beginningless stream that afflicts only the yogin, for the wise one is like an eyeball: a wool thread that hurts the eye does not hurt other limbs. Seeing himself and all beings carried along by it, the yogin takes refuge in right seeing. As medical science has four parts — disease, its cause, health and remedy — so this śāstra has four: saṃsāra, its cause, liberation and the means of liberation. Saṃsāra full of suffering is what is to be avoided; the conjunction of pradhāna and puruṣa is its cause; the final cessation of the conjunction is avoidance; right seeing is the means. The one who avoids cannot himself be rejected (that would be annihilationism) or taken up (that would be causalism); refusing both there is the doctrine of the eternal — this is right seeing.

paraphrase: The seer is the puruṣa, witness of the buddhi; the seen are all things that rise in the buddhi-sattva. The seen, like a magnet, serves by mere proximity and becomes the property of its owner, whose nature is seeing; their beginningless conjunction is the cause of suffering. As one who knows three things — the foot that can be pierced, the thorn that pierces, and the remedy (not treading on it, or wearing a shoe) — avoids the pain, so here. What is pained is sattva, not the unchanging, inactive knower of the field; as sattva is pained, the puruṣa, conforming to its form, is pained as it were.

paraphrase: Sattva has the character of illumination, rajas of activity, tamas of inertia; the guṇas, mutually dependent yet distinct in their powers, are called pradhāna. The seen transforms as the elements and as the senses, gross and subtle, and acts for a purpose: experience and liberation for the puruṣa. Experience is determining the nature of the guṇas as desired or undesired without discrimination; liberation is determining the enjoyer's own nature. Experience and liberation, made by and existing in the buddhi, are ascribed to the puruṣa as victory or defeat of soldiers to their lord; bondage is the buddhi's not completing the puruṣa's purpose, liberation its completion.

paraphrase: The particularized are the five elements (from the five unparticularized tanmātras) and the eleven senses including mind (from unparticularized I-am-ness) — sixteen; the six unparticularized are the five tanmātras and I-am-ness alone; these are transformations of the mere mark, the great principle, pure being; beyond it is the unmarked, the unmanifest pradhāna, neither being nor non-being. The guṇas, conforming to all properties, neither perish nor arise; only their manifestations, with past and future, appear to arise and perish.

paraphrase: The puruṣa is neither of the same form as the buddhi nor entirely different. Not the same: the buddhi changes (its objects are known and unknown), while objects are always known to the puruṣa, which shows he is unchanging; the buddhi exists for another, acting in combination, the puruṣa for himself; the buddhi, having three guṇas, is non-conscious. Nor entirely different: though pure, he beholds the buddhi's cognitions and appears as if of their nature.

paraphrase: The seen, though destroyed for the one puruṣa whose purpose is done, is not destroyed, being common to other puruṣas; for the unskilled its purpose is not done. Hence, since the powers of seer and seen are eternal, their conjunction is beginningless.

paraphrase: Seeing the seen is experience; seeing the seer's own form is liberation; the conjunction lasts until seeing has done its work. Vyāsa then lists the alternative views current in the śāstra on what the non-seeing that causes the conjunction is: the operation of the guṇas; the non-arising of the mind that would show the owner his objects; the purposiveness of the guṇas; ignorance restrained with the mind as the seed of the mind's arising; the manifestation of impressions of motion when those of rest are exhausted; the power of seeing itself; a property of both; seeing (knowledge) itself.

paraphrase: The cause of conjunction is ignorance, the latent tendency of erroneous cognition; the buddhi steeped in it does not reach discernment of the puruṣa and returns with its task unfinished; reaching it, its task done and non-seeing gone, it does not return. [Against a mocking objection — the impotent man who promises a child after his death — a near-teacher replies that liberation is the cessation of the buddhi, which occurs because non-seeing, the cause of bondage, is removed by seeing.]

paraphrase: Discriminative discernment is the cognition of the difference between sattva and puruṣa; while false knowledge has not ceased it wavers. When false knowledge becomes like a burnt, barren seed, the flow of discriminative cognition in sattva, freed of the dust of afflictions and dwelling in the highest lucidity and the highest consciousness of mastery, becomes stainless: that unwavering discernment is the means of avoidance — the path of liberation.

paraphrase: When impurity is gone and no other cognition arises, the discerning one has sevenfold insight. Four are release through insight regarding what is to be done: (1) what is to be avoided is known, nothing more to know; (2) its causes are exhausted, nothing more to exhaust; (3) avoidance is directly realized through the samādhi of stilling; (4) the means of avoidance, discriminative discernment, has been cultivated. Three are release of the mind: (5) the buddhi's task is done; (6) the guṇas, like rocks fallen from a mountain peak, without support, incline toward dissolution in their cause and set with it, never to arise again for want of purpose; (7) in this state the puruṣa, beyond relation to the guṇas, is the light of its own form alone, stainless, alone. Seeing this, the puruṣa is called skilled (kuśala); he remains liberated and skilled even when the mind has dissolved, being beyond the guṇas.

paraphrase: By practising the eight limbs, impurity — fivefold error — dwindles, and as it dwindles the light of knowledge grows, up to discriminative discernment. Practice of the limbs is the cause of separation from impurity, as an axe of what is cut, and of attaining discernment, as dharma of happiness. The śāstra knows nine kinds of cause (of arising, maintenance, manifestation, modification, cognition, attainment, separation, alteration and support); practice of the limbs is a cause in two of these ways only.

paraphrase: Non-harming is not injuring any being in any way at any time; the other restraints and observances are rooted in it and are taught only to perfect and purify it. Truthfulness is speech and mind according to fact, as seen and as inferred; speech is spoken to convey one's understanding, and should be neither deceptive, mistaken nor fruitless, and be for the benefit of all beings, not their harm; spoken to harm beings it is not truth but sin, and by this semblance of merit one reaches painful darkness — so one should speak, after examination, truth that benefits all beings. Stealing is taking another's property otherwise than as scripture allows; non-stealing is its absence, freedom from desire. Celibacy is restraint of the generative organ, with the senses guarded. Non-possessiveness is not appropriating objects, seeing the faults in acquiring, keeping, losing, attachment and harm.

paraphrase: Non-harming limited by class is a fisherman's harming fish only; by place, 'I will not kill at a sacred ford'; by time, 'not on the fourteenth day, not on a holy day'; by occasion, 'only for gods and brahmins', or kṣatriyas' harming only in battle. Unlimited by these, kept in every way, on all grounds and toward all objects without exception, the restraints are called the great vow.

paraphrase: Purity is outer — from earth, water and the like, and eating what is pure — and inner — washing away the stains of the mind. Contentment is not wanting more than the means at hand. Austerity is bearing the pairs of opposites — hunger and thirst, cold and heat, standing and sitting, silence of gesture and of speech — together with vows such as kṛcchra, cāndrāyaṇa and sāntapana as suitable. Self-study is the study of scriptures on liberation or repetition of the praṇava. Devotion to Īśvara is offering all actions to that supreme teacher: 'On bed or seat or walking on the road, self-possessed, the net of harmful thoughts destroyed, seeing the seed of saṃsāra wear away, he is ever yoked and shares in the enjoyment of the immortal.'

paraphrase: When harmful thoughts arise — 'I will kill the one who wronged me; I will lie; I will take his property, lie with his wife, become master of his possessions' — burning with the fever of thoughts bent on the wrong path, one should cultivate their opposites: 'Roasting on the terrible coals of saṃsāra, I took refuge in the dharma of yoga by giving fearlessness to all beings; if, having given up harmful thoughts, I take them up again, I am like a dog' — as a dog licks up its vomit.

paraphrase: Violence is done, caused or approved; each from greed (for meat or skin), anger ('he wronged me') or delusion ('it will be merit for me'); each mild, middling or intense — twenty-seven kinds, which subdivide into eighty-one, and are countless by the variety of beings; so for untruth and the rest. Their fruit is endless suffering and ignorance: the violent man first saps the victim's strength, then causes pain, then takes life; in consequence his own means lose strength, he suffers in hells and as animal and ghost, and, having cut short life, lives on near death each moment, wishing to die yet breathing on, because the painful fruit must ripen; if violence is outweighed by some merit, he gains pleasure but a short life. Reflecting thus on the undesired fruit, one should not set the mind on harmful thoughts.

paraphrase: In one steady in non-possessiveness the wish to know his own condition in past, future and present arises of itself: 'Who was I? How was I? What is this? How is this? What shall we become? How shall we be?' These are the powers from steadiness in the restraints.

paraphrase: When posture is mastered, inhalation is the drawing in of outer air and exhalation the expelling of inner air; the cutting off of their movement, the absence of both, is prāṇāyāma. It is external (absence of movement after exhalation), internal (after inhalation), or a third, stationary one, in which both cease at once through a single effort, as water on a hot stone contracts on all sides. Each is observed by place (its range), time (a measure of moments) and number (of breaths), as mild, middling or intense, and so practised becomes long and subtle. The fourth comes gradually through mastery of the stages, after the spheres of inhalation and exhalation have been ascertained and passed beyond.

paraphrase: For the yogin practising prāṇāyāma, the karma that covers discriminative knowledge dwindles — the karma that, as they say, covers the luminous sattva with a net of illusion made of great delusion and yokes it to what should not be done; binding to saṃsāra, it grows weak through prāṇāyāma and dwindles moment by moment. As it is said: 'There is no austerity higher than prāṇāyāma; from it come purification of impurities and the shining of knowledge.'

paraphrase: When the mind is stilled, the senses, disjoined from their objects, are stilled like the mind, needing no other means as other kinds of sense-mastery do; as bees fly up when the queen bee flies up and settle when she settles, so the senses are stilled when the mind is stilled: this is sense-withdrawal.

paraphrase: Some say mastery of the senses is non-addiction to sounds and other objects — addiction being attachment, which throws one away from the good; [some say it is] lawful enjoyment not contrary [to dharma]; others, contact with objects at will; some, the cognition of objects free of pleasure and pain in the absence of attachment and aversion; Jaigīṣavya: non-apprehension alone, from the mind's one-pointedness. The supreme mastery is this: when the mind is stilled, the senses are stilled and need no further effortful means, as in the other kinds of sense-mastery.

paraphrase: Concentration is the binding of the mind, by its activity alone, to places such as the navel wheel, the lotus of the heart, the light in the head, the tip of the nose, the tip of the tongue, or to an external object.

paraphrase: Saṃyama is applied to the stage next after the one mastered; without mastering the lower stage one does not reach saṃyama on higher stages by skipping. One who has mastered higher stages by the grace of Īśvara need not practise saṃyama on lower ones such as knowledge of other minds, their purpose being achieved otherwise. Which stage follows which — here yoga itself is the teacher; as it is said: 'Yoga is to be known by yoga; yoga proceeds from yoga; one who is heedful through yoga delights long in yoga.'

paraphrase: The transformations described for the mind hold in the elements and senses too. Property-transformation: in the property-bearer the overpowering and appearance of emergence and stilling. Time-mark transformation: stilling, which has three time-marks, leaves the future path and enters the present, where it manifests in its own form without being cut off from past and future (and emergence passes from present to past). State-transformation: in moments of stilling the impressions of stilling grow strong and those of emergence weak.

paraphrase: A property is the capacity of the property-bearer as delimited by its fitness. The property-bearer conforms to properties that have subsided (past), arisen (present) or are not yet determinable (future); since everything has the nature of everything, the not-yet-determinable are all possibilities. For one who holds that there are only properties with no continuant, there could be no experience: how could karma done by one cognition be enjoyed by another, or what one saw be remembered by another?

paraphrase: One property-bearer has different transformations through different sequences (e.g. powder, lump, pot, sherd, particles of clay). The mind's properties are twofold, seen and unseen: the seen are cognitions; the unseen, known by inference, are seven — stilling, merit and demerit, impressions, transformation, life, movement and capacity.

paraphrase: Speech is meaningful only in its sounds; the ear has only the modification of sound for its object; the word is grasped by the buddhi that gathers the sounds. The letters cannot coexist and do not by themselves form the word; the word is one, the object of a single cognition, without parts, without sequence, not made of letters, belonging to the buddhi, called up by the last letter and understood through the convention shaped by beginningless usage; convention is the memory-form of the mutual superimposition of word and meaning.

paraphrase: Through direct perception of his impressions, the blessed Jaigīṣavya saw the sequence of his births through ten great creation-cycles, and discriminative knowledge arose in him. Āvaṭya asked: 'Born again and again among gods and men, and seeing the suffering of hells and animal births, what did you find more — pleasure or pain?' Jaigīṣavya: 'All that I experienced I know to be suffering.' Āvaṭya: 'Is even your mastery over pradhāna and the unsurpassed happiness of contentment on the side of suffering?' Jaigīṣavya: 'That happiness of contentment is unsurpassed only compared with the pleasure of objects; compared with the happiness of kaivalya it is suffering. It is a property of the buddhi-sattva, of the three guṇas, and on the side of what is to be avoided; the thread of craving is suffering, and with the removal of craving's torment this clear, unobstructed, wholly agreeable happiness is spoken of.'
speaker: Jaigīṣavya and Āvaṭya

paraphrase: Karma that ripens as life-span is fast-acting or slow: like a wet cloth spread out, which dries quickly, or rolled up, which dries slowly; like fire in dry grass fanned by wind, or fire set to a heap of grass bit by bit. Omens of death are threefold: personal — not hearing the inner sound with ears closed, not seeing the light when the eyes are pressed; from other beings — seeing Yama's men, or suddenly seeing departed ancestors; from the gods — suddenly seeing heaven or perfected beings, or everything appearing reversed. By these one knows that the end is near.

paraphrase: Friendliness, compassion and gladness are three cultivations (bhāvanā): cultivating friendliness toward the happy one gains the strength of friendliness, and so for compassion and gladness; the samādhi from cultivation is saṃyama, from which come strengths of unfailing force. Equanimity toward the wicked is not a cultivation, so there is no samādhi in it and no strength from it.

paraphrase: The worlds are seven. From the Avīci hell up to the back of Meru is the earth-world (bhūr); from Meru's back to the pole star, the intermediate world of planets and stars; beyond, the heaven-world, the Great Indra's (fivefold); fourth, Prajāpati's world (mahar); and the threefold world of Brahmā — jana, tapas and satya. Below are six great hells (Mahākāla, Ambarīṣa, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Kālasūtra, Andhatāmisra) above Avīci, and seven netherworlds (pātāla); the earth is the eighth, with seven continents around golden Sumeru, surrounded by seven oceans. Classes of gods dwell in each heaven — in Mahendra's world the Thirty-three, the Agniṣvāttas, Yāmyas, Tuṣitas, Aparinirmitavaśavartins and Parinirmitavaśavartins; in Brahmā's worlds the Brahmapurohitas, Brahmakāyikas, Ābhāsvaras, Śuddhanivāsas and others — and those of the highest (satya) world enjoy meditation with reasoning, with reflection, with bliss alone, and with I-am-ness alone. All seven are worlds of Brahmā; the bodiless and those merged in prakṛti, being in the state of liberation, are not placed within the worlds. The yogin is to perceive all this by saṃyama on the sun.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked). Inside the skull is a luminous opening, the light in the head: saṃyama there gives sight of the perfected beings who move between heaven and earth.

paraphrase: The buddhi-sattva, luminous, having subdued rajas and tamas, is transformed into the cognition of the difference between sattva and puruṣa; the puruṣa, pure consciousness, is utterly unlike changing sattva. From saṃyama on the cognition that concerns the puruṣa, which is other [than the cognitions for another's sake] and has pure consciousness as its form, insight about the puruṣa arises; yet the puruṣa is not seen by that cognition, which belongs to the buddhi — the puruṣa sees that cognition, which rests on himself. As it is said: 'By what would one know the knower?'

paraphrase: Intuition and the rest, arising in a concentrated mind, are obstacles, because they oppose that seeing; arising in an emergent mind, they are powers.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Life (jīvana) is the activity of all the senses together, characterized by prāṇa and the rest; its action is fivefold: prāṇa, moving through mouth and nose, operating up to the heart; samāna, which distributes evenly, operating up to the navel; apāna, which carries away, operating down to the soles of the feet; udāna, which leads upward, operating up to the head; and vyāna, the pervading. Prāṇa is chief. From mastery of udāna come non-adherence to water, mud and thorns, and departure at the time of death, which the yogin undertakes at will.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: The eight powers: minuteness (aṇimā) — he becomes minute; lightness (laghimā); greatness (mahimā); reach (prāpti) — he touches the moon with a fingertip; irresistible will (prākāmya) — he rises and dives in the earth as in water; control (vaśitva) over elements and their products, not controlled by others; lordship (īśitṛtva) over their arising, dissolution and arrangement; and the power to settle things as he wishes (yatrakāmāvasāyitva). Though able, he does not overturn the order of things, because the will of another, earlier-perfected one who has that power has already settled the elements so. Earth does not obstruct his body, water does not wet, fire does not burn, wind does not move him; he becomes invisible even to the perfected ones.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Swiftness like the mind is unsurpassed speed of the body; action without instruments is the senses' operating apart from the body in any place, time and object desired; mastery of pradhāna is control over all transformations of prakṛti. These three powers are called 'honey-like' (madhupratīka) and come from mastering the five forms of the senses.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: For the buddhi-sattva cleansed of the dirt of rajas and tamas, in the highest lucidity and the highest consciousness of mastery, established only in the discernment of the difference between sattva and puruṣa, there is sovereignty over all states and knowledge of all, without sequence. This is the power called 'sorrowless' (viśokā); attaining it, the yogin moves about omniscient, the bonds of the afflictions destroyed, in control.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: When he understands that this discriminative cognition is a property of sattva, that sattva belongs among what is to be avoided, and that the puruṣa is unchanging, pure and other than sattva, and becomes dispassionate toward it, the seeds of the afflictions, like burnt rice-seeds, set together with the mind; then the puruṣa no longer experiences the threefold pain; when the guṇas, their purpose done, return to their source, the puruṣa's final separation from the guṇas is kaivalya, the power of consciousness established in its own form.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: There are four kinds of yogin: the beginner (prāthamakalpika), in whom the light has only begun to shine; the one at the honey stage (madhubhūmika), whose insight is truth-bearing; the one whose insight is a light (prajñājyotis), who has mastered elements and senses and guards what has been cultivated; and the one who has passed beyond what is to be cultivated (atikrāntabhāvanīya), whose sole aim is the dissolution of the mind, with the sevenfold final insight. When the brāhmaṇa realizes the honey stage, the gods in their high places, seeing the purity of his sattva, invite him: 'Sir, sit here, enjoy yourself here: this pleasure is lovely, this maiden is lovely, this elixir wards off old age and death, this is a sky-going car, here are wish-fulfilling trees, the holy Mandākinī, perfected beings and great sages, agreeable nymphs, divine ear and eye, an adamantine body — you have earned it all; take this unfading, ageless, deathless place dear to the gods.' Thus addressed he should reflect on the faults of attachment: 'Roasting on the terrible coals of saṃsāra, whirling in the darkness of birth and death, I have somehow found the lamp of yoga that destroys the darkness of the afflictions; these winds of sense-objects born of craving are its enemies. Having found the light, how could I, deceived by this mirage of objects, make myself fuel for the blazing fire of saṃsāra again? Farewell to you, dream-like objects fit for the wretched to crave!' Resolved thus, he should cultivate samādhi. Nor should he be proud, thinking 'I am desired even by the gods'; from pride, thinking himself secure, he will not see that death has him by the hair, and carelessness, always watching for an opening, will find one and stir up the afflictions again — the undesired would recur.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: As the atom is matter at its utmost minuteness, so the moment (kṣaṇa) is time at its utmost minuteness — the time in which a moving atom leaves one point and reaches the next; sequence is the unbroken flow of moments. Moments and their sequence are not an aggregate in reality: hours, days and nights are aggregates made by the buddhi; time, empty of reality, a construction of the buddhi following verbal knowledge, appears to worldly people as a real thing. The moment belongs to reality; only one present moment exists, and the whole world undergoes transformation in that single moment. From saṃyama on moment and sequence comes knowledge born of discrimination.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: 'Deliverer' (tāraka) means arising from one's own intuition, not from instruction; 'having all things as object' — nothing is outside it; 'in all ways' — it knows past, future and present with all their variations; 'without sequence' — it grasps all in one moment. This is complete knowledge born of discrimination; the lamp of yoga, from the honey stage onward, is a part of it.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: When the buddhi-sattva, cleansed of rajas and tamas, has as its only task the cognition of the puruṣa's difference and its affliction-seeds are burnt, it attains as it were the purity of the puruṣa; the puruṣa's purity is the absence of experience figuratively ascribed to him. In that state there is kaivalya — whether for one who has the powers of lordship or for one who has not, whether he has gained knowledge born of discrimination or not; for one whose affliction-seeds are burnt there is no further need of knowledge. In truth, non-seeing ceases through knowledge; then no further afflictions, no fruition of karma; the guṇas, their task done, no longer present themselves to the puruṣa as seen: that is his kaivalya; then the puruṣa is the light of his own form alone, stainless, alone.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Powers from birth: e.g. in a changed body; from herbs: e.g. by elixirs (rasāyana) in the abodes of the asuras; from mantras: flight through space, minuteness and the like; from austerity: fulfilment of will, taking any form at will and going anywhere at will; powers from samādhi have been explained.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Merit and the like do not set the material causes in motion; they only pierce the obstruction, as a farmer who wants to flood another field from a full one does not push the water with his hand but breaks the barrier, and the water flows by itself; or as he removes weeds so that the sap flows into the roots of the grain. So merit is the cause only of the removal of demerit (Nandīśvara is the example); conversely demerit blocks merit (Nahuṣa's becoming a python).
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Created minds are of five kinds, as powers arise from birth, herbs, mantras, austerity and samādhi; only the mind born of meditation is without residue: it has no latent drive of attachment and so no connection with merit or demerit, the yogin's afflictions being exhausted; the others have karmic residue.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Karma is of four kinds: black, white-and-black, white, and neither white nor black. Black belongs to the wicked. White-and-black is accomplished by external means, where accumulation of residue comes through harming and helping others. White belongs to those given to austerity, self-study and meditation: it depends on the mind alone, not on external means, and arises without harming others. Neither white nor black belongs to renunciants whose afflictions are exhausted and who are in their last body: not white, since the yogin renounces the fruit; not black, since he does not take it up. For other beings karma is of the first three kinds.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: The latent tendencies are beginningless, because the self-wish 'may I not cease, may I be', seen in all, is not natural: how could a creature just born, which has not experienced death, fear death except through memory of past pain? Some hold that the mind, like a lamp in a jar or a palace, contracts and expands to the size of the body, which makes the intermediate state and transmigration intelligible; the teacher (ācārya) holds that only the activity of the all-pervading mind contracts and expands. Its causes are external (praise, gifts, salutation, dependent on body and means) and internal (faith and the like, dependent on the mind alone); as it is said: 'the friendliness and the rest, which are the abodes (vihāra) of meditators, independent of external means, bring about the highest dharma'. Of the two the mental is stronger: who could empty the Daṇḍaka forest by bodily action, or drink the ocean like Agastya, without the strength of mind?
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked). 'Vihāra' for maitrī etc. is noted in brw:buddhism-yoga-four-attitudes.

paraphrase: From merit comes pleasure, from demerit pain; from pleasure attachment, from pain aversion; thence effort, by which one, stirring in mind, speech or body, helps or harms others; thence again merit and demerit, pleasure and pain, attachment and aversion: thus turns the six-spoked wheel of saṃsāra, whose driver is ignorance, the root of all afflictions. Cause, result, substrate (the mind with a task) and support hold the latent tendencies together; when these are absent the tendencies are absent.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: [Since the existent cannot perish nor the non-existent arise:] the future is that whose manifestation is to come, the past that whose manifestation has been experienced, the present that which is engaged in its own operation; all three are objects of knowledge — if past and future did not exist in their own form, knowledge of them would be objectless. The property-bearer has many properties arranged by their time-paths; past and future do not exist as the present does, but in their own form, to be manifested or already experienced.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Properties in the three time-paths — present as manifest, past and future as subtle — are forms of the six unparticularized; in reality all this is only a particular arrangement of the guṇas. As the teaching of the śāstra says: 'The highest form of the guṇas does not come within the range of sight; what comes within the range of sight is utterly empty, like an illusion (māyā).'
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked). The quoted verse is attributed by commentators to the Ṣaṣṭitantra / Vārṣagaṇya — attribution from memory, unchecked.

paraphrase: Vyāsa rejects those who, arguing that 'there is no object unaccompanied by cognition, though there is cognition unaccompanied by an object, as in dreams', deny the nature of things and say that the thing is only a construction of cognition, like a dream-object, not real: how can they be trusted, who, by the strength of conceptual cognition that is not a means of knowledge, set aside and deny a thing that presents itself by its own power?
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: One thing, the common support of many minds, is not constructed by one mind or many but stands on its own: the same thing gives rise to pleasure in a mind that depends on merit, pain in one that depends on demerit, delusion in one that depends on ignorance, and indifference in one that depends on right seeing. Some say the object arises together with cognition because it is enjoyed, like pleasure; they deny the thing's being common and its form in earlier and later moments.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: If one mind were grasped by another, by what would the cognition of cognition be grasped? — an infinite regress, and confusion of memories. So the destructionists (vaināśika), denying the puruṣa who is aware of the buddhi, throw everything into confusion. Some of them imagine a mere being that lays down these five aggregates (skandha) and takes up others, and then shrink from it; and saying 'I will live the holy life under a teacher for great disenchantment with the aggregates, for dispassion, for non-arising, for peace', they deny the very being who would do so. The Sāṃkhya, Yoga and other doctrines accept, in their own words, a puruṣa, the owner and enjoyer of the mind.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: The mind, coloured by the object and, being itself an object, joined to the puruṣa by its own activity, appears as both object and subject, conscious and non-conscious, like a crystal. Misled by this, some say the mind itself is conscious; others say 'all this is mind only; there is no world of cows and pots with its causes' — they are to be pitied. The object known in samādhi-insight, reflected there, is other than the insight; so the one by whom it is ascertained is the puruṣa. Those who distinguish grasper, grasping and grasped are the right-seers, and by them the puruṣa is attained.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: As the existence of a seed is inferred from a blade of grass breaking through in the rains, so in one whose hair stands on end and whose tears fall on hearing of the path to liberation, the seed of seeing the distinction — karma leading to liberation — is inferred. In him the natural cultivation of the self's nature — 'Who was I? How was I?...' — proceeds; for the one who sees the distinction it ceases, for he knows that this variety is only the transformation of the mind, and that the puruṣa, in the absence of ignorance, is pure and untouched by the mind's properties.

paraphrase: In the gaps of a mind that flows only with the discernment of the difference between sattva and puruṣa, other cognitions arise from former impressions whose seeds are dwindling: 'I am', 'mine', 'I know', 'I do not know'.

paraphrase: When this brāhmaṇa takes no interest even in the highest reflection and seeks nothing from it, detached even there, he has only discriminative discernment in every way; since the seeds of impressions are exhausted no other cognitions arise: then he has the samādhi called cloud of dharma.

paraphrase: With its attainment the afflictions beginning with ignorance are uprooted and the karmic residues, good and bad, destroyed root and all. When afflictions and karma cease, the wise one is liberated while living — because error is the cause of becoming, and no one whose error has ceased is ever seen to be born anywhere.

paraphrase: Knowledge-sattva, infinite but covered by tamas and only here and there opened by rajas, becomes infinite when freed of all coverings; then what is to be known is little, like a firefly in the sky. As it is said: 'The blind man pierced the jewel; the fingerless threaded it; the neckless wore it; the tongueless praised it.'
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Permanence is twofold: the unchanging permanence of the puruṣa (kūṭastha-nityatā) and the changing permanence of the guṇas (pariṇāmi-nityatā). Is there an end to the sequence of saṃsāra? Some questions are to be answered one-sidedly ('Will all that are born die?' — 'Yes'); some by distinction ('Will all who die be born?' — the discerning one whose craving is exhausted will not, others will; 'Is the human birth better?' — better than animals, not than gods and sages); and 'Is saṃsāra finite or infinite?' is to be answered by distinction: for the skilled there is an end, for others not.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Kaivalya is the dissolution of the guṇas — cause and effect — which have accomplished experience and liberation and are empty of purpose for the puruṣa; or, from the ending of relation with the buddhi-sattva, it is the power of consciousness alone, established in its own form, remaining so forever.
notes: Passage located and read in the GRETIL e-text of Vyāsa's bhāṣya (Ānandāśrama ed.) in sources_raw; paraphrase is a summary by the unit author (skeleton phase; fidelity not yet checked).

paraphrase: Answering the objection that the smṛti names Hiraṇyagarbha, not Patañjali, as the teacher of yoga ('hiraṇyagarbho yogasya vaktā nānyaḥ purātanaḥ'), Vācaspati explains 'anuśāsana' as a teaching that follows (anu) an earlier one: Patañjali re-teaches, he does not originate, the yoga śāstra.

paraphrase: Opening verses: here Vedavyāsa has spoken the essence of the meaning of all the Veda under the guise of the Yoga-bhāṣya — this is the way for those who seek liberation; as the Gaṅgā and other rivers rest in parts of the ocean, so Sāṃkhya and the other darśanas are wholly contained in parts of this.

paraphrase: 'Anuśāsana' is the teaching of what has been taught, showing that the śāstra rests on a teacher: the Yoga-Yājñavalkya teaches that Hiraṇyagarbha is the first teacher ('Hiraṇyagarbha is the speaker of yoga, no other is ancient'). The bhāṣya on the whole śāstra is by the blessed Bādarāyaṇa (Vyāsa), for the good of all. Scripture and smṛti enjoin yoga as a cause of liberation; the Brahma-mīmāṃsā and Sāṃkhya examine knowledge at length but yoga only briefly, so Patañjali sets out yoga in detail.

paraphrase: Against one who says that the result of cognition is a reflection of consciousness (cicchāyā) that belongs to the buddhi alone, Vijñānabhikṣu argues that this abandons the plain sense of the bhāṣya's word 'pauruṣeya', that a mere reflection cannot be a cognition or do the work of illumination, and that, since mutual reflection is established by śruti and smṛti, the result is consciousness itself as qualified by the reflection of the mind's activity.

paraphrase: Ānanda is a particular joy (hlāda) arising from the preponderance of sattva as one ascends from the stage of reflection; in it the mind thinks 'I am happy'. Vijñānabhikṣu rejects the view of 'someone' that hlāda means the senses and that the bliss-samādhi has the senses as its object, and denies any subdivision into 'with bliss' and 'without bliss'. Asmitā is an awareness whose sole object is the self (ekātmikā saṃvit), and is twofold: with the individual self or with the Supreme Self as object. The Mokṣadharma verse on reasoning, discrimination and reflection arising in the first yoga is cited.

paraphrase: Closing the first pāda: in the Sāṃkhya, liberation is taught from knowledge of the principle of the self (jīva) alone, without asamprajñāta yoga; in this śāstra, for a liberation free of obstacles, doubt and delay, knowledge of the Supreme Lord (parameśvara-vidyā) is shown as the swift cause of liberation, together with asamprajñāta yoga.

paraphrase: Samprajñāta samādhi is a special cultivation (bhāvanā), fourfold: savitarka, savicāra, sānanda, sāsmita. What is cultivated is Īśvara or the principles (tattvas). Cultivation on the gross elements and senses with word and meaning mixed is savitarka, without them nirvitarka; on the subtle (tanmātras, inner organ) with place, time and property savicāra, without them nirvicāra — these are 'coalescence with the grasped'. When the inner organ's sattva tinged with rajas and tamas is cultivated, bliss predominates: sānanda — those who rest content here, not seeing pradhāna and puruṣa, are the 'bodiless' (videha); this is 'coalescence with the grasping'. Cultivation on pure sattva, where mere being remains, is sāsmita — asmitā is not ahaṃkāra — and those content here, not seeing the supreme puruṣa, are 'merged in prakṛti'. Those who know the supreme puruṣa and cultivate it have discriminative discernment, 'coalescence with the grasper'. Each stage is left for the next.

paraphrase: The cognition of cessation is the giving up of all thought of reasoning and the rest; its practice is rejecting whatever activity springs up, continuously, as 'not this, not this'; preceded by that, the other samādhi, with only impressions remaining, is asamprajñāta.

paraphrase: Devotion (praṇidhāna) to Īśvara is a special bhakti, a distinguished worship: offering all actions to him, the supreme teacher, without desiring fruits such as sense-pleasure; it is the foremost means to samādhi and its fruit. Īśvara is the special puruṣa who, by his mere wish, is able to lift up the whole world.

paraphrase: Having taught yoga with its means for the concentrated mind, Patañjali now teaches kriyā-yoga for the emergent mind: austerity is kṛcchra, cāndrāyaṇa and the like taught in other śāstras; self-study is repetition of mantras preceded by the praṇava; devotion to Īśvara is offering all actions to the supreme teacher without regard to fruit. The yogin should first be intent on kriyā-yoga.
